title: Why Being Listened to Carefully Can Still Leave You Unseen
deck: Having your feelings soothed is not the same as having your reasons answered; you may still remain unseen as someone capable of judgment.
body: Sometimes someone really is listening to you.
They do not interrupt, can restate your meaning, and can describe your feelings accurately. They know why you are unsettled, which words hurt you, and even how best to respond at this moment.
Yet after the conversation ends, you still feel unseen.
This feeling is hard to explain.
The other person has done what a good listener should do. Your words were not ignored, and your feelings were soothed. Why is that still not enough?
Perhaps because what was heard was only your state of mind, not your judgment.
You say, “I don’t want to continue this arrangement, because it keeps leaving the risk with me.”
The other person replies, “I know you’ve been under a lot of pressure lately. That’s why you’re so sensitive.”
They have heard the pressure but have not addressed the risk.
You say, “This isn’t what I want.”
They say, “You’re just afraid of change.”
They have heard fear, but have not acknowledged that not wanting something may itself be a reason to take seriously.
Someone can understand your emotions in great detail while treating your reasons as products of those emotions.
You are thus taken seriously as someone who needs soothing, but not as someone capable of judgment.
This is an absence that is hard to notice.

If listening serves only to calm someone down, it decides in advance that the conversation’s goal is to restore the original arrangement. Every feeling can be accepted as long as it does not change the conclusion in the end.
You may be sad, afraid, or temporarily resistant. Once those emotions have been dealt with, you are expected to return to the direction already prepared for you.
This kind of listening seems gentle, but in fact leaves your words no chance to change the relationship.
Truly seeing someone does not mean agreeing with every judgment they make.

Their reasons may be insufficient, and their facts may be wrong. Taking their judgment seriously does not mean abandoning your own, but first treating their reasons as something that might require you to change your view.
You may still disagree in the end.
But before disagreeing, you need to answer the question they actually raised, not merely explain why they raised it.
“I know you’re afraid” cannot replace “Does the risk you point out exist?”
“I understand you’re hurt” cannot replace “Does my behavior need to change?”
“I know you haven’t been doing well lately” cannot automatically dismiss “Is this arrangement fair?” either.
Seeing someone means allowing their reasons into your judgment, not merely into your routine for offering comfort.

Sometimes this will only enable you to explain more clearly why you still cannot agree. Sometimes it will force you to revise a conclusion you were sure of. Whatever the outcome, the other person can feel that their words were not merely received, but helped shape what happens next.
There is another common kind of listening in relationships.

Someone waits patiently for you to finish, but what they are really waiting for is their turn. They prepare their rebuttal in their mind, fitting every sentence of yours into their own reply. When you finish, they can repeat it accurately, but have never allowed a single sentence to interrupt their original course.
It is not that they have failed to hear the voice, but that they have not allowed it to have an effect.
Of course, we cannot demand that everything we express must change the other person.

No one automatically gains the power to make others obey simply by earnestly stating their reasons. Being seen does not mean being approved, and being respected does not mean always getting the outcome you want.
The difference lies in whether the other person has actually answered your reasons, explained why they still disagree, and left their conclusion open to further revision through facts and actions.
A simple “No, I still disagree, because…” can sometimes show more respect than many gentle words of comfort.
At least it acknowledges that the person before you is not a bundle of emotions waiting to be calmed, but someone who has offered a judgment.
We long to be seen not only because we want others to know we are hurting.
We also want the things our pain points toward to be examined seriously, and our “why” not to be treated as an obstacle requiring treatment.
Real listening does two things at once.
It is willing to care for the person speaking and to let their reasons put pressure on the original arrangement.
It does not assume a reason must be right because an emotion is strong, nor that the presence of emotion means the reason no longer counts.
The moment of being seen is not necessarily when someone says, “I understand you completely.”
It is more likely when they pause, look again at something they had considered settled, and say:
“I don’t agree with you yet, but I know I can no longer pretend your reasons haven’t changed the question.”
entry_door: This essay uses no theoretical terms, but behind it lies the same question: how can a relationship draw close to someone without living their life for them? To follow this line of thought further, start with Non Dubito in Five Minutes.
